identification.summary: Rancor is a cyber espionage group that Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 first described on 26 June 2018. Unit 42 found it through attacks in Southeast Asia during 2017 and 2018, work that grew out of its research into the KHRAT Trojan [S1][S2]. Unit 42 said the group used two main malware families, DDKONG and PLAINTEE, against targets in countries including Singapore and Cambodia. Because the decoy documents drew on political news, Unit 42 judged that the group was targeting political entities [S1]. Check Point later tracked a seven-month Rancor spear-phishing campaign against Southeast Asian government entities, and Unit 42 reported repeated attempts against a Cambodian government organization using new custom malware called Dudell [S3][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: 2017. Unit 42 observed DDKONG in use from February 2017, and the earliest known PLAINTEE sample dates to October 2017 [S1][S2]. Check Point describes the group as active since at least 2017 [S3][S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft (Typhoon) name for Rancor appears in the sources gathered. Palo Alto Networks tracks the group as Rancor Taurus, and the ETDA threat encyclopedia also lists the names Rancor Group and Rancor Taurus [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Rancor (G0075) and describes it as operating in Southeast Asia with politically themed lures [S9]. Secondary coverage reports Kaspersky-identified links between Rancor and DragonOK, and a link to the KHRAT operators, whom Unit 42 has associated with DragonOK. These are overlaps between clusters, not evidence that Rancor and DragonOK are the same group [S2][S10].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected China-nexus. ETDA lists the country as China [S10], and CFR's Cyber Operations Tracker describes Rancor as a China-linked group [S8]. Check Point said its 2019 report contained insights that 'might indicate' a Chinese origin [S3][S4]. No government attribution appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate, vendor-only. Check Point's wording is hedged ('might indicate') [S3]. Unit 42 notes that Derusbi, which Rancor used, is believed to be unique to a small subset of Chinese cyber espionage groups [S6]. A Unit 42 analyst quoted by CyberScoop said Rancor's tools are all custom, either unique to Rancor or shared with a small cluster of Chinese espionage groups [S7].
attribution.basis: Malware overlap with a small set of China-associated groups (Derusbi; links to KHRAT and DragonOK) [S6][S7][S2]; Check Point's origin indicators [S3]; and consistent targeting of Southeast Asian governments and political entities [S1][S3].

objectives: Espionage against Southeast Asian governments and political entities [S1][S3][S10]. Unit 42 inferred the political focus from decoys built on public political news, including material linked to the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party [S1]. ETDA lists the group's motivation as information theft and espionage [S10].

targeting.notes: Cambodia appears in every major reporting window: decoys hosted on a Cambodian government website in 2018 [S1], and persistent attempts against a Cambodian government organization from December 2018 to January 2019 and again in mid-2019 [S6][S7]. Check Point reported five unnamed government targets in the region, according to secondary coverage [S4]. Unit 42 said the attempts against the Cambodian organization appear to have failed [S7].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing is the main way in. Unit 42 did not see the original 2018 emails and inferred them from the decoy documents found on infected systems [S1]. In 2018, delivery used HTA files and DLL loaders that downloaded further malware and displayed decoy images or PDFs hosted on legitimate sites, including a Cambodian government website and, at least once, Facebook [S1]. The payloads were DDKONG and PLAINTEE, and PLAINTEE communicates over a custom UDP protocol [S1][S2]. In the 2018-2019 campaigns, the group sent Excel and other Office documents with macros, exploited known vulnerabilities, and sent lures from real government email accounts [S3][S4][S5]. It also used DLL side-loading through trusted signed executables [S3]. Unit 42 reported a new custom macro-based malware, Dudell, and attempts to install Derusbi or KHRAT [S6]. MITRE also records msiexec use to fetch installers over HTTP, certutil for tool transfer, scheduled-task persistence, and HTTP C2 [S9].

campaigns.name: DDKONG / PLAINTEE operations (Clusters A and B)
campaigns.summary: DDKONG was in use from February 2017, and PLAINTEE samples appeared from October 2017. Unit 42 linked two activity clusters through PLAINTEE. They targeted political entities in Singapore and Cambodia with HTA and DLL-loader lures.

campaigns.name: Unit 42 public disclosure of RANCOR
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 named the previously unidentified group RANCOR and published details on DDKONG, PLAINTEE, and decoys hosted on a Cambodian government website.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government spear-phishing campaign
campaigns.summary: From December 2018 to June 2019, Check Point tracked lures sent to government departments and embassies. The lures were updated over time, sent from real government email accounts, and used macros and known exploits to install backdoors.

campaigns.name: Attempts against a Cambodian government organization (Dudell)
campaigns.summary: From December 2018 to January 2019, the group sent weaponized Excel documents (Dudell) and tried to install Derusbi or KHRAT. A further script-based attempt followed in July 2019. Unit 42 said none of the attempts appear to have succeeded.

diamond.adversary: Rancor (Unit 42: Rancor Taurus), a suspected China-nexus espionage group. Vendor-only attribution [S1][S3][S10].
diamond.capability: Custom malware: DDKONG, PLAINTEE (custom UDP C2) and Dudell. Shared families: Derusbi and KHRAT. Delivery and execution via HTA, DLL loaders, side-loading, Office macros, known exploits, msiexec and certutil [S1][S3][S6][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Decoys hosted on legitimate sites, including a Cambodian government website and Facebook [S1]. Compromised or abused real government email accounts used as senders [S5]. HTTP-based C2 [S9].
diamond.victim: Government departments, embassies and political entities in Cambodia, Singapore and the wider Southeast Asia region [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Lures built from regional political news, including Cambodian opposition (CNRP) themes, around a period of Cambodian political tension. This points to collection of political intelligence on Southeast Asian governments [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Microsoft Office with macros enabled or unpatched against known vulnerabilities. Trust in signed executables, which enables side-loading [S3][S9].

gaps: Primary documents could not be opened: WebFetch failed to resolve unit42.paloaltonetworks.com, research.checkpoint.com, cfr.org, thehackernews.com, cyberscoop.com and securityaffairs.com. Report details come from search-result excerpts of those pages.
The publication date of the Unit 42 Dudell report (S6) is listed as 2019-12-17 in search-result metadata; the exact date of the CyberScoop article (S7) was not confirmed beyond December 2019.
No Microsoft threat actor name for Rancor was found. Mapping to the Microsoft taxonomy is unverified.
No activity reported after 2019 was found in reliable sources. A secondary blog's claim that Dudell was 'discovered in 2024' conflicts with Unit 42 and was not used.
The Rancor/DragonOK/KHRAT relationship is stated only in secondary coverage of Kaspersky and Unit 42 research. The Kaspersky source itself was not located.
No government (USG or allied) attribution or sponsoring-agency identification (e.g., MSS or PLA unit) was found.
Thailand and Vietnam come from secondary sources (Security Affairs, ETDA) and are not confirmed in a primary vendor report reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant terrain is Southeast Asian partner-nation government networks, embassies and political-party systems, especially Cambodia and Singapore, plus the legitimate government websites and email accounts the actor abuses for staging and delivery [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Partner ministries' trust in mail from real government accounts weakens email-based defenses. This affects US engagement and coalition planning that runs through these partners [S3][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is a politically themed spear-phishing document (HTA, macro Excel or exploit document), then a loader or DLL side-load, then a custom backdoor (DDKONG, PLAINTEE, Dudell, Derusbi or KHRAT) with HTTP or custom UDP C2 and scheduled-task persistence [S1][S3][S6][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained, iterative phishing of partner ministries and embassies to collect political intelligence, retargeting after failed attempts [S3][S7]. MDCOA is compromising partner-government mail accounts and websites to send lures to US or coalition personnel engaged in the region. That second scenario is extrapolated from observed account and website abuse, not from reported targeting [S1][S5]. Candidate indicators: Office documents spawning msiexec or certutil downloads over HTTP; new schtasks /create entries; signed binaries loading DLLs from user-writable paths; unusual outbound UDP from workstations; decoys pulled from government or Facebook URLs [S1][S3][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track partner-nation reporting and vendor feeds on Southeast Asian government phishing. Rancor reporting is sparse after 2019, so lack of reporting does not mean the group is inactive [S3][S6]. (2) Authorities: The victims are mainly foreign partner governments [S1][S3]. Defensive support is a matter for partner-engagement and information-sharing arrangements rather than DODIN authorities, except where DoD personnel or systems receive lures. (3) Mission assurance: Mission-partner and embassy-adjacent DoD users should treat mail from partner-government accounts as possibly compromised, and macro and HTA execution controls should be enforced [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: Coordinate with interagency and partner CERTs (for example, Cambodian and Singaporean) to share decoy hashes and abused legitimate URLs. Attribution remains vendor-only and hedged, so products should describe it that way [S3][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: The Rancor group’s attacks use two primary malware families which are naming DDKONG and PLAINTEE. DDKONG is used throughout the campaign and PLAINTEE appears to be new addition to these attackers’ toolkit. Countries Unit 42 has identified as targeted by Rancor with these malware families include, but are not limited to Singapore and Cambodia.
